title: Asking the Mud to Bring Her Home
hook: a lotus pond drained in summer, all mud, and a hymn that asks the mud itself to bring the goddess home
carry: the lotus: fortune rising clean from the mud
tomorrow: what does a hymn of a thousand names call the goddess first?

segments.voice: Yesterday counted truth of speech among its riches: Lakshmi is more than money. Today, she's asked to stay for good, and a week ends.

Drain a lotus pond in the dry season and you don't find anything pretty. You find mud, thick and dark, with old roots running through it like cables. But that's where the flower lives. Every bloom draws on what's down there in the dark. The Sri Sukta has been calling the lotus goddess all week. And when it finally asks her to move in for good, it doesn't ask the flower to do the inviting. It asks the mud.
screen: `DRAIN THE POND. FIND MUD.` → `THAT'S WHERE THE FLOWER LIVES.` → `THE HYMN ASKS THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Through Kardama she has children. Kardama, come and dwell with me. Make Sri, the mother garlanded with lotuses, dwell in my family. Kardama is a name, and as a word it means mud. Tradition hears him as her son. So the singer asks her own child to move in, so his mother will follow. The next line does the same with water. In paraphrase: may the waters bring forth soft and gentle things. Chiklita, live in my house, and make the divine mother Sri dwell in my family. Chiklita, tradition says, is another of her children, linked to moisture. Mud and water: the two humble things a lotus can't live without. He doesn't ask the gold or the elephants to bring her, but the plainest, dampest parts of the earth. And this is why Lakshmi is called Padma and Kamala, both names for the lotus, and why she's pictured seated on one. Hindus love the lotus for what it does: it roots in mud and rises clean, water sliding off its leaves. Many teachers read it as a picture of a good life: grown out of ordinary, messy ground, and not stained by it. Notice the word family, too. Not my house only, but my people, across generations, some readers say. That's this week: a guest welcomed, a goddess who fills others, I choose you, a vow's heat, Alakshmi shown the door, riches wider than money, and now the mud. The hymn goes on a little further, but this is where the path leaves it. Tomorrow, a different hymn, one that praises the goddess by her names.
screen: `KARDAMA, WHOSE NAME MEANS MUD.` · `CHIKLITA, AND THE WATERS.` · `PADMA, KAMALA: THE LOTUS ONE.` · `DWELL IN MY FAMILY.` · then, large: `THE LOTUS RISES CLEAN FROM THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something plain that holds your life up: a hard season you came through, a parent's ordinary work, the early mornings. Then notice what has grown out of it that you're glad of now, and rest with the two together, root and flower. If you pray, you can thank the goddess, or God, for both; if you don't, let the plain thing be honored for once.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn that calls Sri near, chooses her, and finally asks Kardama, the mud, to bring the lotus mother home to stay.
Your line: the lotus, fortune rising clean from the mud. Mud and water, asked to bring her home. Go gently.

chat.meaning: Kardama, whose name means mud, is heard as Sri's son. The singer asks mud and water, what a lotus needs, to bring her home. The lotus rises clean from the mud.

Kardama.meaning: a name that means mud; tradition hears him as Sri's son

Chiklita.meaning: another of Sri's children in tradition, linked to moisture

Sri Sukta.meaning: the hymn to Sri, the goddess of fortune

Padma.meaning: lotus; a name of Lakshmi, like Kamala

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verses 11–12 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)

notes: Verse 11 paraphrased: kardamena prajābhūtā mayi sambhava kardama / śriyaṃ vāsaya me kule mātaraṃ padmamālinīm. Verse 12: āpaḥ sṛjantu snigdhāni ciklīta vasa me gṛhe / ni ca devīṃ mātaraṃ śriyaṃ vāsaya me kule. 'Through Kardama she has children' is a simplification of kardamena prajābhūtā; confirm.
Kardama and Chiklita as Sri's sons, and Chiklita's link to moisture, are traditional readings, attributed to tradition. 'Kardama means mud' is lexical. Confirm.
